Every oxidation rate that oxidizr computes depends on measurements, on
constants, and on physiological assumptions. This vignette explains each source
of error, shows how to propagate measurement uncertainty, how to see which
source matters most, and which statistic to report.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(oxidizr)
```

## Three kinds of error

- **Measurement error.** VO2, VCO2, isotope enrichments, urea and body mass
  are measured with some error. It can be **random** (it differs from one
  observation to the next) or **systematic** (it shifts every subject in the
  same direction: an analyser calibration, the enrichment of the drink, the
  mean background enrichment of a separate control group).
- **Choice of constants.** The fat equation depends on the lipid chosen as
  representative, the gas volumes on the molar volume, protein on its formula
  or general values. These are model choices, not measurement errors
  (`vignette("stoichiometry")`).
- **Physiological assumptions.** Steady state, no bicarbonate degassing, no
  net gluconeogenesis or ketone accumulation. The package explains them but
  cannot propagate them (see the last sections).

Random errors average out over subjects, and the between-subject SD already
contains them. Systematic errors do not average out, and no SD, SE or CI across
subjects shows them, so oxidizr reports them apart (`<var>_u_sys`).

## Why CHO and fat amplify gas errors

CHO and fat oxidation are differences of two large terms in VO2 and VCO2, so a
small error in one gas gives a large relative error in the rates. Each 1% error
in VCO2 gives about 3% error in the share of energy from CHO (Elia & Livesey,
1992, p. 125), and the share of energy from CHO and fat is about 12 times more
sensitive to errors in the non-protein RQ than energy expenditure is (Livesey &
Elia, 1988). Correlation between the two gas errors matters as much as their
size:

```{r}
k <- stoich_coefficients
vo2 <- 2.5
vco2 <- 2.3
cho <- k$cho_vco2 * vco2 + k$cho_vo2 * vo2
fat <- k$fat_vo2 * vo2 + k$fat_vco2 * vco2

# Independent 1% errors in VO2 and VCO2 (for example, gas fractions)
u_cho <- sqrt((k$cho_vco2 * vco2 * 0.01)^2 + (k$cho_vo2 * vo2 * 0.01)^2)
u_fat <- sqrt((k$fat_vco2 * vco2 * 0.01)^2 + (k$fat_vo2 * vo2 * 0.01)^2)
round(100 * c(cho = u_cho / cho, fat = u_fat / fat), 1)   # % of each rate

# A 1% error shared by both gases (for example, flow or volume)
round(100 * c(cho = abs(cho) * 0.01 / cho, fat = abs(fat) * 0.01 / fat), 1)
```

`oxidation_uncertainty()` therefore has separate sources for each gas (`vo2`,
`vco2`) and for an error they share (`volume`).

## Typical input uncertainties

These values come from the literature. Use them to choose the uncertainties of
your own measurements, or better, measure them (replicates, control trials).

| Input | Typical value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| VO2, best case | 0.5% | Livesey & Elia (1988), p. 610 |
| VO2 and VCO2, metabolic carts, between days (CV) | 0.5-3.2% and 0.7-5.0% | Van Hooren et al. (2026) |
| VO2 and VCO2, error of commercial carts against a simulator | 1-18% | Van Hooren et al. (2023) |
| Breath δ13C by IRMS | 0.06-0.1‰ | Gautier et al. (1996); Pettersson et al. (2020) |
| Plasma glucose δ13C by LC/IRMS (SD) | 0.7-0.9‰ | Godin et al. (2011); Morrison et al. (2011) |
| Drink δ13C (Rexo) near 205-211‰ | 1.0-2.0‰ | Godin et al. (2011) |
| Resting breath δ13C, SD of rest samples (6 subjects, 3 occasions) | 0.4-0.5‰ | Wagenmakers et al. (1993) |
| Background breath δ13C, within one subject | 0.21-0.25‰ | Gautier et al. (1996) |
| Background rise from rest to exercise | 0.2-2‰ | Wagenmakers et al. (1993); Gautier et al. (1996) |
| Protein oxidation from urinary N | +14 to -39% | Livesey & Elia (1988) |
| Body mass (scale tolerance) | about 100 g | Cheuvront & Montain (2017) |

## Propagating measurement uncertainty

The example below simulates a crossover study: 8 subjects, a glucose trial
(Rexo 75‰) and a water trial, two time points, three replicate measurements of
VO2 and VCO2 at each.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
ids <- 1:8
prots <- c("Glucose", "Water")
calo <- expand.grid(id = ids, protocol = prots, time = c(60, 90), rep = 1:3,
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
calo$vo2 <- 2.5 + rnorm(nrow(calo), 0, 0.05)
calo$vco2 <- 2.3 + rnorm(nrow(calo), 0, 0.05)
calo$rep <- NULL

rexp <- expand.grid(id = ids, protocol = prots, time = c(60, 90), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
background <- rnorm(8, -24, 0.5)
rexp$rexp <- background[rexp$id] + ifelse(rexp$protocol == "Water", 0.3, 9)

study <- OxidationStudy(
  calorimetry = CalorimetryData(data = calo, protocol_col = "protocol"),
  isotopes = IsotopeData(rexp = rexp, rexo = data.frame(protocol = prots, rexo = c(75, NA)),
                         protocol_col = "protocol", rpla = NULL),
  urea = NULL, environment = NULL, subjects = NULL
)
```

By default, `analyze_oxidation()` propagates only what the data show: with
`aggregate = TRUE`, the SD of the replicates of each mean (SD / sqrt(n)); with
13C data, the SD of the background enrichment in the control trials. Here we
also state an analysis precision of 0.1‰ for Rexp and 0.2‰ for Rexo:

```{r}
u <- oxidation_uncertainty(rexp = 0.1, rexo = 0.2)
u

res <- analyze_oxidation(study, aggregate = TRUE, control_protocol = "Water",
                         validate = FALSE, uncertainty = u)
glucose <- res@oxidation_rates$protocol == "Glucose"
head(res@oxidation_rates[glucose, c("id", "time", "cho_total", "cho_total_u",
                                    "cho_exo", "cho_exo_u", "cho_exo_u_sys")])
```

Each variable has `<var>_u`, its standard uncertainty, and `<var>_u_sys`, the
part that is systematic. The default method is first order (GUM): each source
moves its input by one standard uncertainty, the calculations run again, and the
change is the contribution of that source. It is exact for the linear CHO and
fat equations.

## Which source matters most

`uncertainty_budget()` ranks the sources of one variable:

```{r}
uncertainty_budget(res, "cho_exo", by = "protocol")
```

For exogenous CHO, the background enrichment dominates: every subject gets the
control-group mean Rref, but their own background differs from it. How this
error behaves depends on the design:

- **Crossover** (each subject also did the control trial, as here): the mean
  contains the subject's own background, so the error is SD × sqrt(1 - 1/n),
  random (`rref_subject`), and nothing is shared across subjects.
- **Parallel groups** (the control trials come from other subjects): the error
  is SD, random (`rref_subject`), plus the uncertainty of the group mean,
  SD / sqrt(n), which shifts every subject in the same direction
  (`rref_mean`, systematic).

In a crossover study, take each subject's Rref from their own control trial
(`rref_by_subject = TRUE`). The between-subject spread then leaves the error;
what is left is the within-subject variation of the background, about 0.25‰
(Gautier et al., 1996):

```{r}
own <- analyze_oxidation(study, aggregate = TRUE, control_protocol = "Water",
                         validate = FALSE, rref_by_subject = TRUE,
                         uncertainty = oxidation_uncertainty(rexp = 0.1, rexo = 0.2,
                                                             rref = 0.25))
c(group_rref = mean(res@oxidation_rates$cho_exo_u[glucose]),
  own_rref = mean(own@oxidation_rates$cho_exo_u[glucose]))
```

When a result is not linear in its inputs (for example exogenous CHO when
Rexo - Rref is small, or rates near 0, where they are cut at 0), check the first
order result with Monte Carlo propagation (GUM Supplement 1):

```{r}
set.seed(2)
mc <- analyze_oxidation(study, aggregate = TRUE, control_protocol = "Water",
                        validate = FALSE,
                        uncertainty = oxidation_uncertainty(rexp = 0.1, rexo = 0.2,
                                                            method = "monte_carlo",
                                                            n_draws = 200))
c(linear = mean(res@oxidation_rates$cho_exo_u[glucose]),
  monte_carlo = mean(mc@oxidation_rates$cho_exo_u[glucose]))
```

## Choosing constants

The constants are a model choice. `compare_constants()` runs the analysis with
the defaults, then with each other option of each part, one at a time:

```{r}
cmp <- compare_constants(study, vars = c("cho_total", "fat_total"),
                         aggregate = TRUE, control_protocol = "Water")
cmp[c("set", "cho_total_mean", "fat_total_mean")]
```

The molar volume moves the results most: with the real-gas volumes of Péronnet &
Massicotte (1991), glucose has an RQ of 0.996. Across published equations, CHO
oxidation varies by up to 6% (Jeukendrup & Wallis, 2005, Table 3) and fat
energy by up to 17% (Elia & Livesey, 1992, Table 19). This spread is not added
to the propagated uncertainty: report it apart, or state the constants you used
(`res@constants`). See `?oxidation_constants` for each option and its source.

## Exogenous glucose: the 13C assumptions

- **Background rise.** The background enrichment of expired CO2 rises during
  exercise: by 0.83‰ at 60% and 0.99‰ at 75% VO2max in European subjects
  (Gautier et al., 1996). In Dutch subjects who avoided foods from C4 plants,
  the rise did not exceed 0.3‰, against 1-2‰ in North American studies
  (Wagenmakers et al., 1993). With natural enrichment, exogenous oxidation was
  overestimated by 37-53% with a resting background and by about 35% with an
  exercise water trial as background (Massicotte et al., 1993);
  Péronnet et al. (1990) found 10-20% with an exercise water trial. Take Rref
  from a control trial during exercise, and prefer a high enrichment of the
  drink, which makes the background change negligible.
- **CO2 recovery.** During exercise, recovery of labelled CO2 is practically
  complete (Telmosse, 2022, pp. 75-76), so oxidizr applies no correction.
- **Equilibration delay.** Labelled CO2 passes through the bicarbonate pool.
  Estimates of the time to equilibrium range from 25 min (Gonzalez & King,
  2023) to 60 min (Moseley et al., 2005); Telmosse (2022, p. 77) excludes data
  before 40 min. Use `time_range` to exclude early data.

## Assumptions the package cannot propagate

- **Steady state.** Indirect calorimetry needs a steady state; use
  `detect_steady_state()` and `filter_steady_state()`.
- **RER above 1.** Hyperventilation or acidosis releases CO2 from the
  bicarbonate pool; indirect calorimetry is then not valid (Telmosse, 2022,
  pp. 56-57). oxidizr sets negative rates to 0, and `validate_study()` flags
  high RER.
- **Protein from nitrogen.** General factors can be wrong by +14 to -39%
  (Livesey & Elia, 1988); a change in the urea pool hides urea (Elia &
  Livesey, 1992, p. 94). State a `protein` uncertainty if protein matters.
- **Other.** Skin CO2 loss (1-2% of CO2 output), ketone accumulation and
  colonic fermentation also bias the RQ (Livesey & Elia, 1988, Appendix).

## Which statistic to report

| Statistic | What it describes | In oxidizr |
|---|---|---|
| SD | How subjects differ | `error = "sd"` |
| SE = SD / sqrt(n) | Precision of the group mean | `error = "se"` |
| CI (t, n - 1 df) | Range for the group mean, at `level` | `error = "ci"` |
| `<var>_u` | Uncertainty of one subject's value from the inputs | `analyze_oxidation(uncertainty = )` |
| `<var>_u_sys` | Error shared by all subjects (calibration, drink enrichment, a separate control group's mean Rref) | reported apart in summaries |

Summaries use the subject as the unit: each subject's rows are averaged first,
so n counts subjects, not observations. Do not add `<var>_u` to the SE of a
group mean: the random part is already in the between-subject SD. Report the
systematic part apart:

```{r}
summarize_oxidation(res@oxidation_rates[glucose, ], vars = "cho_exo", level = 0.95)
tbl_oxidation_summary(res, by = "protocol", error = "ci")
```
